title: A Case of the Mondays: That's a Lot of D for a Tuesday
seoTitle: Commanders 22, Bengals 20: The Defense Shows Up, Antonio Williams Breaks Loose and Drew Stevens Walks It Off
summary: Commanders 22, Bengals 20 on Monday night: three sacks of Joe Burrow, Chase and Higgins held to 74 yards, Antonio Williams in 46 seconds, Drew Stevens' walk-off and a defense that finally showed up.
paragraphs: It's Tuesday. I know. The column is called A Case of the Mondays, and the NFL put our game on Monday night, which means I'm filing a Monday column on a Tuesday with a Monday hangover from a Tuesday morning. The schedule makers did this to me. I'd complain, but I don't have a complaint in me today. The D kept me up past my bedtime, and I regret nothing.

On Sunday I wrote Commanders 35, Bengals 30, for the only reason I had, which was that I said so. Final: Commanders 22, Bengals 20. Right winner, off by 23 points, and I'll take it. I had the shootout wrong because I didn't account for the one thing nobody on ESPN accounted for either. The Bengals flew into Landover expecting a little D. They got all of it.
## That's a Lot of D

I want to talk about the D. I've wanted to talk about the D all season, and for about nine weeks there wasn't much to talk about. Monday night, the D was everywhere. The D was in Joe Burrow's face before he finished his first cadence. The D was waiting at the line on fourth-and-1. The D spent three hours in the rain slapping the best receiver duo in football around, and the receiver duo did not care for it. Joe Burrow has seen a lot of D in his career. He has never seen D like this. Nobody has. It was so much D that at one point the stadium lights gave out, and I'll get to that.

Tim Settle Jr. gave Joe Burrow the D on the very first snap of the game. Not the first drive. The first play. Joe hadn't even gotten comfortable yet. Then Settle gave it to him again in the second quarter, and Tashan Reed credited the coverage on that one, which is the polite way of saying everybody got involved. Three sacks on the night for a quarterback whose protection, according to John Keim before kickoff, had been outstanding. Joe looked very relaxed in the pocket right up until the pocket had a Settle in it.

Then there's the fourth down. First quarter, Bengals facing fourth-and-1, and Zac Taylor dials up a Burrow keeper, which is a bold thing to run at a defense that has been waiting its whole life for this moment. Frankie Luvu met him at the line like he'd read the play call off a napkin. Turnover on downs. The team account tweeted "WHAT A STOP BY THE DEFENSE" in all caps, and for once the caps lock was earned. Joe Burrow tried to sneak past the D and the D said, not tonight, sweetheart.

Here's the stat that made me sit up. Per Keim, Washington blitzed 12 times in the first half and recorded 11 pressures overall, and Daronte Jones ran three safeties for most of the half. Three safeties. That's a lot of D in one place. That's technically a D party, and Daronte Jones sent the invitations. The zero blitz, for the uninitiated, is when all of the D comes at you at once, with nobody held back. Mike Gesicki said afterward that the constant zero-blitz look made it tough. Mike. Buddy. That's the idea. The D is supposed to make it tough. If it were easy, it wouldn't be the D.

And the receivers. On Sunday I wrote that Ja'Marr Chase would do something Monday night that ended up on every highlight show for a week. Ja'Marr Chase caught five passes for 31 yards. Tee Higgins got 43 and a touchdown. Seventy-four yards, combined, for the two best receivers in the sport. Burrow's explanation: "They pretty much double-teamed Ja'Marr and Tee every play." Joe, when two guys are on you every single play, that's not a scheme anymore. That's a lifestyle. Chase's take was that we "just really did our normal." Ja'Marr. Five catches. Thirty-one yards. You took the D for three hours and now you don't even want to talk about it. That's fine. We'll talk about it for you. We haven't given up 24 points in five straight games. This IS the normal now. You just hadn't experienced the D yet.

One more, because I can't help myself. The Bengals ran the ball for 31 yards. Not on a play. On the night. Thirty-one rushing yards, 4-for-12 on third down, 312 total yards for the hottest offense in football. That's what happens when the D is this big and this everywhere. There's nowhere to go. You just stand there in the rain and take it.

Was it perfect? No. Samaje Perine took a checkdown 44 yards on third-and-11 after Burrow escaped the pressure, and the very next thing that happened was Higgins catching a 31-yard touchdown on his first target of the night, which Ben Standig called an excellent adjustment and I called several other things. Gesicki hurt us all night, five catches for 77 yards, most of them with a man draped on him. Rasul Douglas had two near-interceptions and the SS Impala had a third that Bengals.com said he probably should have picked. Nobody picked anything. The Bengals didn't turn it over once. The D held them to 20 points anyway, their fewest since Week 2, and ended a five-game winning streak. Trey Amos said after the game that this defense is really starting to click. Trey, we noticed. The whole stadium noticed. Joe Burrow noticed most of all, and he's going to be noticing it in the film room all week.
## 32 Yards in 28 Minutes

Now the other side of the ball, where for 28 minutes the D was going the other direction. Our first four drives: 15 plays, 27 yards, four punts. Boye Mafe gave Jayden the D three times before halftime, a career high for him and a personal low for me, and he did it in the time it takes to microwave a burrito. JP Finlay, at the two-minute warning: "Commanders have 32 yards of offense at the 2 min warning of the first half. 28 minutes of game, 32 yards." It was raining the entire time. Standig: "The weather people lied about the rain going away." Everybody lied to us, JP. Everybody.

Then ESPN's cameras found Stefon Diggs on the sideline, and Diggs, with the tact of a man who has caught a lot of footballs, yelled, "Throw the [word I can't print on a site my mother reads] ball!" Reader, they threw the ball. Tashan Reed had the perfect summary: they threw it, and they didn't punt for the rest of the game. Down 10-0 with 1:55 left in the half, Jayden ran for 10 on third-and-9, hit Chig Okonkwo for 32 yards down to the 6, Treylon Burks drew a pass interference in the end zone, and Jacory Croskey-Merritt, in his first game back from injured reserve, punched it in from the 1 behind Sam Cosmi, who took out two Bengals on one block. 10-7 at the half, and we had the ball coming out. Four punts, then six straight scoring drives of 50 yards or more, which ESPN Research says no team has done to end a game in 45 seasons. Somewhere, Diggs is taking credit, and he should.
## Then the Lights Went Out

The first play of the second half, basically, was Jayden Daniels running 47 yards, the longest run of his career, which also moved him past RG3 for second all-time in franchise history in quarterback rushing yards. And then the lights went out. Actually went out. In the stadium. With Roger Goodell in the building. Northwest Stadium saw Jayden run 47 yards through a Bengals defense and fainted, which is the most honest review our offensive line has gotten all year. Also, and I'm just saying, it was dark, it was raining, and there was a tremendous amount of D on the field. Somebody was going to need a minute.

When the lights came back, Drew Stevens kicked a 36-yarder to tie it, and then the night turned into the Drew Stevens show. Burrow went 7-for-7 on a drive that ended with a Colbie Young touchdown to make it 17-10, and from there we answered with field goals. Forty yards. Twenty-five yards, after a 13-play drive stalled at the 7, which I'm still a little mad about. Forty-one yards on fourth-and-1 from the 24 to take a 19-17 lead with 2:26 left. Chris, I know. I know. Last week you said "4th and less than 1. Go for it," and I'm sure you said it again Monday, probably louder. They kicked. It worked. I'm not relitigating it on a Tuesday.
## Forty-Six Seconds

Here's where the D came back for one more. Burrow threw a jump ball to Gesicki for 32 yards, and I made a noise I didn't know I could make. Then, on third down with the Bengals already in field goal range, Nick Cross came on a blitz and gave Joe one last helping of D, a seven-yard sack that Tashan Reed called "a terrible play by Burrow" while giving Cross the credit he deserved. It turned a comfortable kick into a 56-yarder. Evan McPherson made it anyway, because of course he did. 20-19, Bengals, 46 seconds left, and we had no timeouts.

Forty-six seconds. From our own 28. Jayden to Antonio Williams for 22. Jayden to Antonio Williams for 42, down to the 8, with the rookie breaking loose and the entire offense, linemen included, sprinting downfield to line up and spike it. Jayden, afterward, on the big guys having to run: "They better bring their ass down there." They brought it. Spike. Drew Stevens from 26, no time left. Commanders 22, Bengals 20. Dan Quinn, afterward: "What I told the team in the locker room is this is a team win."

Antonio Williams finished with nine catches for 122 yards, his first 100-yard game, and 93 of those came in the fourth quarter, the most by a rookie in a fourth quarter since 2020. Jayden threw for 143 yards in the first three quarters and 146 in the fourth. He finished 23-of-35 for 289 and ran for 55 more, and he did it against the MVP favorite on a Monday night in the rain, for the second time. Jayden Daniels is 2-0 against Joe Burrow on Monday Night Football. I didn't believe The Athletic's headline either. Forgot what Jayden Daniels can do? I didn't forget. I just hadn't seen it in a while.
## Drew Stevens Wants Kids

Five field goals. Thirty-six, 40, 25, 41, 26. A Bills reporter noted that some of Stevens' kicks looked awkward and low all night, and that's fair, and also none of them missed, so I'm going to need the Bills reporter to mind his own kicker. Then John Keim asked Stevens how he handled the pressure, and Drew Stevens said this: "I want to have kids. Am I going to tell my kids their dad was a little [Keim censored the word, and I'm going to respect that]? Or am I going to tell my kids, yeah, your dad walked out there and he drilled it and he was ready for it." Drew. Sir. There are children present. Also, he drilled it. Tell the kids.

The other quote that got me was Quinn's, on why this one meant more. The scars from our late-game losses run deep, he said, and he was glad Jayden won it for us. We've lost this exact game three or four times this season. Against the Rams it ended in laterals. Monday night, with 46 seconds and no timeouts, it ended in a spike and a kick. Quinn said before the game it would come down to critical situations and complementary football, which is coach for "the D has to hold and the offense has to show up." Both happened. In the same game. I'm as surprised as you are.
## Ref Watch: Bill Vinovich

My note on Sunday was that Vinovich's crews throw a league-average 13.2 flags a game, and that both times he's had us, we drew more flags than the other guys. That's us, not him. Monday night: ten flags total, five on them for 39 yards and five on us for 40. Dead even, under his average, and by my own system, which is that I get mad when they flag us and call it beautiful when they flag them, this was a perfectly adequate night of officiating that I have no feelings about, which for me is a personal best. The flag that mattered most was the pass interference on Treylon Burks in the end zone, which moved us to the 1 and set up the only touchdown we scored. The flag I enjoyed most came in the first quarter, when a Bengals rusher knocked an official over with our quarterback and the official threw it from the seat of his pants, which is a level of commitment I respect.

The controversy, such as it is, belongs to Cincinnati. The Athletic reports the Bengals should have had two more seconds after our go-ahead field goal, but the rules say the officials can't put time back on the clock after a review when the next play is a kickoff. So the clock operator, reportedly, cost the Bengals one more play. Bengals fans, I understand. I've been you. I've been you for 30 years. Welcome to the club, the dues are your soul. Ref Watch updates when the crew for Sunday is announced, so I can start getting mad in advance.
## Sideline Report

The building was a scene. Alex Ovechkin stood behind the kicking net in an 8 jersey watching Jayden throw, then did a walk-and-talk with Jason Kelce, which is a sentence I'd like framed. Ovi came to see the D. He's a hockey player. He knows a D-man when he sees one, and he saw eleven. John Riggins was there, again, and Standig's full review was "Good." Jonathan Allen spent pregame catching up with old teammates and then spent the game, per Keim, feasting inside because Dexter Lawrence gets doubled 81 percent of the time. Jon, we see you. We still love you. Please go home now.

At midnight, the team account wished Sonny Styles a happy birthday, which means the SS Impala spent the first part of his birthday almost intercepting Joe Burrow. And the team's official postgame tweet, I am not making this up, was "come for the locker room speech, stay for the Beer Spears." I asked for the beer spear. I said so on Sunday. The franchise listens to me and nobody else, and I'm starting to think that's the problem.
## Meanwhile, in Charlottesville

You got the full UVA report on Sunday: 41-24 over North Carolina, bowl eligible, and Tony Elliott now 2-0 against Bill Belichick. I wrote that if Tony Elliott can beat Belichick twice, Dan Quinn can beat Joe Burrow once. I'd like that entered into the record. I'd also like it noted that the President's Box has a roof, and Northwest Stadium does not, and that my wife's job has better weather. This weekend it's the Hokies in Blacksburg, where there is no roof and no box and no mercy. Beat Tech.
## Call Your Shot

Four of you picked this one, and every single one of you who picked us had a shootout. Punch came closest at 28-27, off by 13, right winner. CryoGen went 31-27, off by 16, right winner. skel called 27-34 Bengals and gets points for honesty and nothing else. My 35-30 was off by 23, which is the most I've missed by all season and also the happiest I've been about a miss. None of us saw the D coming. In fairness, neither did Cincinnati.

Season standings: I'm still in first at 3-2, averaging 9.6 points off, and Punch is 2-for-2 and coming for me on the [leaderboard](leaderboard.html). The Cardinals poll is open now. The D will be on the field. Plan accordingly.
## Next Up

We're 4-5-1. Three weeks ago we were 2-5-1 and I was writing about curtains. Now we've won two in a row for the first time since 2024, and Ryan Dunleavy points out something I'd missed: the Giants are two games up at 6-3-1, but we hold the tiebreaker, and because of the tie, no other team can hold one over them. The NFC East, which stinks, has gotten a lot more interesting. Josina Anderson spent her postgame yelling at Colin Cowherd in all caps about everyone who called for Quinn's job, which was a public service and also very funny.

The Cardinals are Sunday. Thanksgiving is Thursday. I plan to spend it the way the Bengals spent Monday night: surrounded by D, slightly overwhelmed, and not entirely sure what just happened. Here's the hope part, because there's always a hope part. For five weeks I've been telling you the defense was coming together, and for five weeks you've nodded politely. Monday night it came together on national television against the best offense in football, and the Bengals went home sore. The D showed up. Keep bringing it. Hail.

wireTaps: Who gave Joe Burrow the D best: Settle on the first snap, Luvu on fourth-and-1, or Cross with the game on the line?
